paragraph: On the morrow, as every one sat around Rama but none spoke, Bharata finally said, "My mother is pacified, for heeding her wishes you gave me the kingdom. I now give it back to you. You alone can command Kosala. Just as a donkey cannot keep pace with a horse, or a small bird with that great Tarkshya, I too have not the power to emulate you. Blessed is the life of him whom others depend upon for their sustenance, but cursed is he who depends on others, for his! Let the subjects of Ayodhya behold you being installed king of Ayodhya, like the resplendent sun." All those who had assembled there applauded Bharata's decision but Rama disagreed. Trying to reason with Bharata, Rama said, "Bharata! Man is not independent of divine will nor is he master of his fate, for destiny is inexorable. Wealth amassed can vanish and lofty positions can crumble. Every union ends in separation and life ends in death, just as every fruit that ripens has no other fear except that of falling from the tree. For every man born, there is no other fear than death. The strongest homes built on mighty pillars, fall to ruin, as time passes on and so do those who grow old and perish with age. In this world days and nights pass quickly decreasing the life of all just as the rays of the merciless sun dry up the waters.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Bharata, having ostensibly 'pacified' his mother, formally renounces the kingdom and attempts to return it to Rama, acknowledging his own inadequacy to rule compared to Rama. He articulates a desire for self-reliance and for Rama to assume his rightful position. However, Rama disagrees, delivering a profound philosophical discourse on the impermanence of life, the power of destiny, and the inevitability of change, separation, and death, using various metaphors to illustrate his point.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Bharata's action is to unequivocally hand back the kingdom to Rama, emphasizing humility and the natural order. Rama's action is to refuse the throne by teaching Bharata about the transient nature of worldly possessions and relationships, the supremacy of 'divine will' or 'destiny', and the ultimate reality of death. This is a key teaching on detachment and the acceptance of life's natural course.
Outcome/Resolution: Bharata's attempt to restore the kingdom is unsuccessful, as Rama firmly adheres to his commitment to his father's decree. The dialogue establishes Rama's profound philosophical outlook on life and duty, which will guide his refusal of the throne. The immediate outcome is a stalemate on the issue of Rama's return.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Karma (Destiny/Fate - 'destiny is inexorable', 'man is not independent of divine will')
Anitya (Impermanence - 'Wealth amassed can vanish', 'Every union ends in separation', 'Life ends in death')
Vairagya (Detachment/Non-attachment - implicit in Rama's discourse on impermanence)
Dharma (Duty - Bharata's plea from his understanding of dharma, Rama's adherence to his vow)
Samsara (Cycle of birth and death - implicit in 'every man born, there is no other fear than death')
Tarkshya (Garuda, symbol of speed and power, used by Bharata for comparison)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Spiritually, the passage delves into profound philosophical truths of 'Karma' (destiny) and 'Anitya' (impermanence). Rama asserts that human will is subordinate to 'divine will' or 'destiny,' and that all worldly phenomena—wealth, positions, unions, and life itself—are transient, eventually dissolving into 'separation' and 'death.' This discourse serves as a teaching on 'Vairagya' (detachment), encouraging acceptance of the natural cycles of existence. Bharata's initial spiritual act of renouncing the throne is met with Rama's deeper spiritual wisdom on the nature of reality.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Bharata expresses a feeling of hopelessness and inadequacy, stating he 'cannot emulate' Rama and feels 'cursed' if dependent. This reflects low self-esteem in relation to Rama's capabilities. Rama's response serves as a profound stress management and emotional regulation technique. He does not directly address Bharata's self-perception but shifts the focus to the universal truths of impermanence and destiny. By emphasizing that 'man is not independent of divine will' and that 'every union ends in separation and life ends in death,' Rama encourages acceptance of inevitable life changes, thereby psychologically preparing Bharata (and himself) to cope with loss and the unpredictable nature of existence, potentially alleviating anxiety related to control and worldly attachments.
